title: Next Year, Don't Start With Belonging
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart pushes back on the common instinct to open a school year by cultivating student belonging directly — telling reluctant readers they're "readers" or math-avoidant students they're "mathematicians." He argues belonging sits at the top of the Five Key Beliefs pyramid for a reason: it's the byproduct of doing the harder work below it (Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy), not a starting point teachers can manufacture with icebreakers and team-building games. Drawing on responses to his own outreach to secondary educators, he singles out schools that lead with belonging-and-community language as diagnosing the motivation problem backwards. He points to his own book's chapter proportions as physical evidence of the argument — only one of ten strategies in The Will to Learn is dedicated to Belonging, because the other nine beliefs generate it as a side effect. The piece is a compact argument for sequencing motivation work correctly rather than jumping to the belief that feels most emotionally urgent to address first.
points: Reframes belonging as an outcome of Credibility, Value, Effort, and Efficacy work rather than a standalone intervention teachers can install directly at the start of a year.
Critiques the common school-culture move of leading with "belonging and community" language as misdiagnosing why students disengage in the first place.
Uses the disproportion in his own book (only 1 of 10 strategies devoted to Belonging) as structural evidence for where belonging actually sits in the motivational stack.
Argues that icebreakers and team-building activities can't manufacture belonging in a class students don't already find valuable, well-scaffolded in effort, or credibly taught.
quotes: Belonging and community are critical to human flourishing — no doubt about it. But folks typically don't get much flourishing juice out of belonging to groups of people they really don't want to belong to.

You can play all the get-to-know-you games you want, do a thousand ice breakers, and use every team-building activity on the Internet, but unless your class has something that I believe is Valuable, unless you've made clear to me what kinds of Effort will help me grow…I'm still going to be watching the clock until I can leave.
This is why Belonging is at the top of the Five Key Beliefs pyramid. If you take care to do specific things that cultivate the four key beliefs below, Belonging is easy to put in place on top.
Once those beliefs are in place, now you can point out to the student that he's a reader, that she's a mathematician. Because now you've got PROOF.
See how small the Belonging section is? That's on purpose. Only one of the 10 strategies I unpack in the book focuses on Belonging.
